subject: moon snail
title: That Perfect Hole in a Seashell Was Drilled by a Killer Snail

scenes.text: That perfect round hole in a seashell isn't an accident. Something drilled it.
The driller is a moon snail. It plows through the sand, finds a clam, and wraps it in its huge, slimy foot.
Then it goes to work. It softens the shell with acid and scrapes at it with a tongue covered in teeth.
A Lewis's moon snail grinds through about half a millimeter a day. One clam can take four days.
When the hole is through, it slides in a straw-like mouth and eats the clam inside its own shell.
The hole it leaves is beveled, like a countersunk screw. Check the next shell you pick up.

description:
The neat round hole you find in seashells on the beach was drilled by a predator.
Moon snails (family Naticidae) hunt clams and other snails under the sand. A moon snail wraps its prey in its large foot, softens a spot on the shell with acid and enzymes from a special boring organ, and scrapes the softened shell away with its radula, a tongue-like ribbon of teeth. Lewis's moon snail of the Pacific coast of North America, which grows to 14 cm, drills about half a millimetre a day, so an average kill takes around four days; other species can finish in hours to a couple of days. It then pushes its tube-like mouth through the hole and eats the animal inside. The hole is perfectly circular with bevelled sides, which is how you can tell a moon snail made it, and moon snails drill other moon snails too. Drilling snails like these have been around for at least 200 million years.
Have you ever found a shell with a hole like this? Comment below.
first_comment: Moon snails drill other moon snails too. Have you ever found a shell with one of these holes?
